paragraphs.title: Warning About Covenant-Breaking and Israel's Leadership

easy.explanation: The passage begins, “Set the trumpet to thy mouth.”
easy.q: What was the prophet commanded to use as a warning?

easy.explanation: The verse says they had “transgressed my covenant, and trespassed against my law.”
easy.q: What had Israel transgressed and trespassed against?

easy.explanation: The passage says, “the enemy shall pursue him.”

answers: Because they violated God's covenant and law
medium.explanation: The enemy comes because Israel transgressed the covenant and law.
medium.q: Why was danger coming upon Israel?

answers: The building of a new temple
medium.explanation: The eagle image emphasizes the speed and danger of the approaching enemy.
medium.q: What does the eagle coming against the house of the LORD suggest?

answers: Israel cries to God but rejects what is good
Israel builds altars but does not pray
Israel turns to Assyria but remains in Egypt
medium.explanation: Israel says, “My God, we know thee,” yet has “cast off the thing that is good.”
medium.q: What contrast appears in these verses?

answers: A cry alone does not remove the consequences of wrongdoing
The enemy has no connection with Israel's conduct
Israel has already defeated the enemy
challenge.explanation: Although Israel cries out, it has rejected goodness, and the enemy still pursues it.
challenge.q: What is shown by placing Israel's cry to God beside the enemy's pursuit?

answers: A new king is being appointed
challenge.explanation: The trumpet is commanded in the context of imminent danger and covenant-breaking.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from the command to blow the trumpet at the beginning of the passage?

answers: As leadership needing warning because it turned from goodness
As leadership unrelated to the enemy
challenge.explanation: Israel violated the covenant, trespassed against the law, and rejected what was good.
challenge.q: How is Israel's leadership portrayed in this passage?

paragraphs.title: Kings, Idols, and the Calf of Samaria

answers: They set up kings and princes
easy.explanation: The passage says, “They have set up kings, but not by me: they have made princes.”
easy.q: What did Israel do without God's approval?

easy.explanation: The verse says, “of their silver and their gold have they made them idols.”
easy.q: What did Israel use to make idols?

easy.explanation: The passage says, “the workman made it; therefore it is not God.”
easy.q: Who made the calf of Samaria?

answers: They acted without God's approval and made idols
medium.explanation: They appointed leaders without God and used silver and gold to make idols.
medium.q: Why were Israel's actions wrong according to the passage?

medium.explanation: The silver and gold were made into objects of false worship.
medium.q: What does the word “idols” refer to in this passage?

answers: It would be broken in pieces
It would continue ruling the people
It would be rebuilt in Judah
medium.explanation: The passage says, “the calf of Samaria shall be broken in pieces.”
medium.q: What would happen to the calf of Samaria?

answers: The appointment was not approved by God
The kings were appointed by the prophet
challenge.explanation: The phrase denies that the appointments came from God's authority or will.
challenge.q: What does “but not by me” emphasize concerning the appointment of kings?

answers: The wealth invested in idols could not protect them from destruction
The wealth guaranteed that the idols would remain
The silver and gold were used to build cities
challenge.explanation: Despite the investment of precious metals, the idols and calf would be destroyed.
challenge.q: What connection exists between the silver and gold and the destruction of the idols?

answers: It was made by a workman and was not God
It was too far from Samaria
It was made from material that was too valuable
challenge.explanation: The passage stresses that a workman made it and that it was not God.
challenge.q: What is the central criticism of the calf of Samaria?

paragraphs.title: Sowing Wind, Dissolving Among the Nations, and Foreign Dependence

easy.explanation: The verse says, “they have sown the wind.”
easy.q: What did Israel sow according to the image in the passage?

easy.explanation: The passage continues, “they shall reap the whirlwind.”
The verse says, “they are gone up to Assyria.”

answers: Empty actions will bring a severe result
Good labor will bring a great harvest
medium.explanation: The image describes severe consequences rather than a useful harvest.
medium.q: What does sowing the wind and reaping the whirlwind mean?

answers: A vessel that is unwanted or useless
medium.explanation: Israel is compared to an unwanted vessel among the nations.
medium.q: What does “a vessel wherein is no pleasure” mean in context?

answers: By hiring lovers and depending on rulers
medium.explanation: The passage describes Israel going to Assyria and hiring lovers among the nations.
medium.q: How did Israel try to form relationships with foreign powers?

answers: Dependence on foreign nations brings exile closer
Turning to foreign nations removes every danger
The relationships immediately return Israel home
challenge.explanation: Israel's foreign alliances and dependence contribute to its coming judgment.
challenge.q: What is the connection between Israel's turning to foreign nations and its exile?

answers: Israel's actions will produce no useful or lasting result
challenge.explanation: The agricultural image emphasizes the absence of a productive result.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from the phrase “it hath no stalk”?

answers: Empty actions, absorption among the nations, and dependence on foreigners
Keeping the law, building a temple, and gaining victory
Offering sacrifices, receiving forgiveness, and returning
challenge.explanation: The passage moves from sowing wind to being swallowed among the nations and seeking foreign help.
challenge.q: What sequence is described in verses 7–10?

paragraphs.title: Many Altars and the Rejection of Torah and Sacrifice

easy.explanation: The verse says, “Ephraim hath made many altars.”
The passage says, “they were counted as a strange thing.”
easy.q: How were the great things of God's law regarded?

easy.explanation: The verse says, “the LORD accepteth them not.”
easy.q: Did the LORD accept their sacrifices?

answers: They did not contain enough silver
medium.explanation: The passage says, “altars shall be unto him to sin.”
medium.q: Why did the many altars not help Ephraim?

answers: Sacrifices offered by the people but not accepted by God
Sacrifices burned with an especially large fire
medium.explanation: The people offered flesh, but the LORD did not accept their sacrifices.
medium.q: What does “the sacrifices of mine offerings” refer to in context?

answers: God would remember their iniquity and visit their sins
The people would receive immediate forgiveness
The sacrifices would cancel the law
medium.explanation: The LORD would remember their iniquity and visit their sins.
medium.q: What would follow the sacrifices that were not accepted?

answers: They multiplied religious practices while treating the law as strange
They studied the law while avoiding worship
They built no altars and knew nothing of the law
challenge.explanation: The passage contrasts many altars with counting God's law as a strange thing.
challenge.q: What contrast appears between the many altars and the people's attitude toward the law?

answers: Performing a ritual does not guarantee acceptance before God
Eating the sacrifices was the main thing God desired
The sacrifices removed the people's sins
challenge.explanation: They ate the flesh, but the LORD did not accept the sacrifices and remembered their sins.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from the fact that the people ate the sacrifices but the LORD did not accept them?

challenge.explanation: The passage ends by saying, “they shall return to Egypt.”
challenge.q: Where did the people ultimately turn according to the end of the passage?

paragraphs.title: Forgetting God and the Destruction of Human Works

easy.explanation: The verse says, “Israel hath forgotten his Maker.”
The verse says, “Judah hath multiplied fenced cities.”

answers: They would be moved to Assyria
medium.explanation: The LORD says, “I will send a fire upon his cities, and it shall devour the palaces thereof.”
medium.q: What would happen to Judah's cities and palaces?

medium.explanation: Fenced cities were strengthened for defense.
medium.q: What does “fenced” mean in the phrase “fenced cities”?

answers: Human construction could not protect the people from the fire
The buildings caused Israel to return to Egypt
medium.explanation: Even the temples and fortified cities would not prevent destruction.
medium.q: What is the connection between the buildings and the judgment?

answers: The people invested in their own works while forgetting their Maker
The people remembered God through every building
The people stopped building after forgetting God
challenge.explanation: The verse places Israel's forgetting of its Maker beside its building of temples.
challenge.q: What contrast is emphasized between forgetting God and building many structures?

answers: The warning and judgment concern both parts of the people
Only Judah was guilty of building
challenge.explanation: Israel forgot its Maker, while Judah multiplied fortified cities; both are included in the warning.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from mentioning both Israel and Judah?

answers: Human works cannot save people when God is forgotten
challenge.explanation: Despite the temples and fortified cities, fire would consume the cities and palaces.
challenge.q: What is the main message of the chapter's conclusion?
